title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 139 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 661–665 (Night 139, continuing directly from nights-138), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 139 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The Great Chamberlain, now sultan of Baghdad as al-Malik Sāsān, hears Kān Mā Kān's verses and has Nuzhat al-Zamān shut her niece Qaḍā Fakān away from him. Kān Mā Kān and his mother leave the palace for a poor quarter at the edge of the city; Qaḍā Fakān sends word, and two lines of verse, that she loves him as much as he loves her. At seventeen, penniless and unable to see her, he slips out of Baghdad at dawn barefoot, with a seven-year-old felt cap and a three-day-old loaf, and his mother's lament for him moves the whole city, until the news reaches King Sāsān. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirty-ninth night,
sentences.n: The small alif over the lām of thalāthūn is the print's own: it spells the word without its long alif (والثلٰثون).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْحَاجِبَ الْكَبِيرَ لَمَّا صَارَ سُلْطَانًا سَمَّوْهُ الْمَلِكَ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ḥājiba al-kabīra lammā ṣāra sulṭānan sammawhu al-malika sāsāna
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the chamberlain the great, when he became sultan, they named him al-Malik Sāsān.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the Great Chamberlain became sultan, he was given the name al-Malik Sāsān, King Sāsān.
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd into the next word (السعيدان). The sentence starts with the Chamberlain and then turns to “they named him”, a loose but common shape: the subject is set at the head and taken up again by the pronoun. Sāsān is the legendary ancestor of the Persian Sasanian kings, so the name is a grand one for a usurper.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ عَلَى تَخْتِ الْمَمْلَكَهِ وَسَارَ فِى النَّاسِ سِيرَةً حَسَنَةً
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa ʿalā takhti al-mamlakati wa-sāra fī al-nāsi sīratan ḥasanatan
sentences.l: And he sat on the throne of the kingdom and went among the people a going good.
sentences.i: He took his seat on the throne of the kingdom and ruled the people well.
sentences.n: takht, a Persian word, “throne”. The print writes mamlaka with a plain hāʾ for its final tāʾ marbūṭa (المملكه), and fī with a dotless yāʾ (فى). sāra fī al-nās sīratan ḥasanatan, “he went among the people a good going”: sīra, “way of acting, conduct”, is the verbal noun of sāra, “to go”, used as its own object.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ جَالِسٌ يَوْمًا إِذْ وَصَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ أَبْيَاتُ كَانَ مَاكَانَ فَنَدِمَ عَلَى مَا فَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa jālisun yawman idh waṣalat ilayhi abyātu kāna mā kāna fa-nadima ʿalā mā fāta
sentences.l: And while he was sitting one day, behold, there reached him the verses of Kān Mā Kān, and he regretted what had passed.
sentences.i: One day, as he sat in state, the verses of Kān Mā Kān came to his ears, and he regretted what was past.
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … behold”: the usual way of bringing in something that happens suddenly. The print runs mā into kāna in the hero's name here (ماكان). nadima ʿalā mā fāta, “he regretted what had gone by”: presumably that he had let the cousins grow up together so freely.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَ عَلَى زَوْجَتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ إِنَّ الْجَمْعَ بَيْنَ الْحَلِفَةِ وَالنَّارِ لَمِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْأَخْطَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhala ʿalā zawjatihi nuzhati al-zamāni wa-qāla inna al-jamʿa bayna al-ḥalifati wa-al-nāri la-min aʿẓami al-akhṭāri
sentences.l: And he went in to his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān and said: Truly the bringing-together between the esparto-grass and the fire is indeed of the greatest of the dangers.
sentences.i: He went in to his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān and said, “To put dry grass beside fire is among the greatest of dangers.
sentences.n: A proverb, in rhyme (nār, akhṭār). ḥalifa, as the print points it (الحَلِفة), is a single stalk of ḥalfāʾ, esparto or halfa grass, a dry grass that catches at once. la-min, “indeed among”: the lām of emphasis after inna.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَتِ الرِّجَالُ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ بِمُؤْتَمَنِينَ مَادَامَتِ الْعُيُونُ تَرْمُقُ وَالْجُفُونُ تَخْنُقُ
sentences.tr: wa-laysati al-rijālu ʿalā al-nisāʾi bi-muʾtamanīna mā dāmati al-ʿuyūnu tarmuqu wa-al-jufūnu takhnuqu
sentences.l: And the men are not, over the women, trusted-ones, as long as the eyes cast-glances and the eyelids strangle.
sentences.i: Men are not to be trusted with women so long as eyes steal glances and eyelids slay.
sentences.n: laysa … bi-, “is not …”: bi- merely strengthens the negated predicate. muʾtaman ʿalā, “trusted with”. The print runs mā into dāmat (مادامت), “as long as”. More rhyme: tarmuqu, takhnuqu. ramaqa, “to look at, to glance at”. takhnuqu, “strangle”, is odd with jufūn, “eyelids”; perhaps the languid lids of the beloved are said to choke the lover, or perhaps it is a slip for takhfiqu, “flutter” (تخفق, one dot different). It is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّ ابْنَ أَخِيكِ كَانَ مَاكَانَ قَدْ بَلَغَ مَبْلَغَ الرِّجَالِ فَيَجِبُ مَنْعُهُ عَنِ الدُّخُولِ عَلَى رَبَّاتِ الْحِجَالِ وَمَنْعُ بِنْتِكِ عَنِ الرِّجَالِ أَوْجَبُ لِأَنَّ مِثْلَهَا يَجِبُ أَنْ تُحْجَبَ
sentences.tr: wa-inna ibna akhīki kāna mā kāna qad balagha mablagha al-rijāli fa-yajibu manʿuhu ʿani al-dukhūli ʿalā rabbāti al-ḥijāli wa-manʿu bintiki ʿani al-rijāli awjabu li-anna mithlahā yajibu an tuḥjaba
sentences.l: And truly the son of your brother Kān Mā Kān has reached the reaching-point of the men, so it is binding to keep him from the going-in upon the ladies of the bridal-curtains; and the keeping of your daughter from the men is more-binding, because the like of her must be veiled.
sentences.i: Your brother's son Kān Mā Kān has come to man's estate, and he must be kept from going in among the ladies of the curtained rooms; and it is still more needful to keep your daughter from men, for a girl like her should be veiled.”
sentences.n: More rhyme: rijāl, ḥijāl. balagha mablagha al-rijāl, “he reached the reach of men”: he is grown. rabbāt al-ḥijāl, “mistresses of the curtains”: ḥijāl is the plural of ḥajala, the curtained canopy of a bride, so the phrase means high-born, secluded women; the print marks the doubled bāʾ (ربّات). bintiki, “your daughter”: Qaḍā Fakān is Sharrukān's daughter, but Nuzhat al-Zamān has raised her. yajib, “it is binding”, and awjab, “more binding”, play on the same root; tuḥjab, “she be screened”, on the root of ḥājib, the Chamberlain's own title.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ صَدَقْتَ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ الْعَاقِلُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ṣadaqta ayyuhā al-maliku al-ʿāqilu
sentences.l: And she said: You have spoken-truly, O king the wise.
sentences.i: She said, “You are right, O wise king.”

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ الْغَدُ جَاءَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ عَلَى جَرْيِ عَادَتِهِ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى عَمَّتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهَا فَرَدَّتْ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna al-ghadu jāʾa kāna mā kāna ʿalā jaryi ʿādatihi wa-dakhala ʿalā ʿammatihi nuzhati al-zamāni wa-sallama ʿalayhā fa-raddat ʿalayhi al-salāma
sentences.l: And when was the morrow, came Kān Mā Kān according to the running of his custom, and he went in to his aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān and greeted her, and she returned to him the greeting.
sentences.i: Next day Kān Mā Kān came as he always did, went in to his aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān and greeted her, and she returned his greeting.
sentences.n: ʿalā jaryi ʿādatihi, “on the running of his habit”: as usual. ʿamma, “paternal aunt”: Nuzhat al-Zamān is his father's sister. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”; the print marks the doubled lām (سلّم).

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي عِنْدِي كَلَامٌ مَاكُنْتُ أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَقُولَهُ وَلٰكِنْ أُخْبِرُكَ بِهِ رَغْمًا عَنِّي فَقَالَ لَهَا قُولِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu yā waladī ʿindī kalāmun mā kuntu uḥibbu an aqūlahu wa-lākin ukhbiruka bihi raghman ʿannī fa-qāla lahā qūlī
sentences.l: And she said to him: O my child, with me is a speech which I was not loving that I should say it, but I inform you of it in spite of me. And he said to her: Say.
sentences.i: She said to him, “My son, I have something to say that I would rather not say; but I must tell it to you, though it goes against my will.” He said, “Tell me.”
sentences.n: The print runs mā into kuntu (ماكنت). akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. raghman ʿannī, “in spite of me”, against my wish: the spoken form of the Classical raghman ʿalayya or ʿalā raghmī. waladī, “my child”, is an aunt's affectionate address.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ إِنَّ أَبَاكَ الْحَاجِبَ أَبَا قَضَى فَكَانَ قَدْ سَمِعَ بِمَا أَنْشَدْتَهُ فِيهَا مِنَ الشِّعْرِ فَأَمَرَ بِحَجْبِهَا عَنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat inna abāka al-ḥājiba abā qaḍā fakāna qad samiʿa bi-mā anshadtahu fīhā mina al-shiʿri fa-amara bi-ḥajbihā ʿanka
sentences.l: And she said: Truly your father the chamberlain, the father of Qaḍā Fakān, has heard of what you recited about her of the poetry, and he commanded the screening of her from you.
sentences.i: She said, “Your father the Chamberlain, Qaḍā Fakān's father, has heard of the verses you have recited about her, and he has ordered that she be kept from your sight.
sentences.n: The Chamberlain is neither Kān Mā Kān's father nor Qaḍā Fakān's: she is the daughter of Sharrukān, he the son of Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and the Chamberlain is only the husband of the aunt who has brought them up. Nuzhat al-Zamān may be speaking loosely, of the man who stands to both as a father in her house, or the text has slipped; it is kept as printed. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”; amara bi-, “to order”: bi- marks what is ordered. ḥajb, “screening, veiling”, again plays on the title ḥājib.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا كَانَ يَا وَلَدِي لَكَ عِنْدَنَا حَاجَةٌ فَأَنَا أُرْسِلُهَا إِلَيْكَ مِنْ وَرَاءِ الْبَابِ وَلَا تَنْظُرْ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَلَا عُدْتَ تَرْجِعُ هُنَا مِنْ هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā kāna yā waladī laka ʿindanā ḥājatun fa-anā ursiluhā ilayka min warāʾi al-bābi wa-lā tanẓur qaḍā fakāna wa-lā ʿudta tarjiʿu hunā min hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: So if there is, O my child, for you with us a need, then I send it to you from behind the door; and do not look at Qaḍā Fakān, and do not again come back here from this time.
sentences.i: So if you have need of anything from us, my son, I will send it out to you from behind the door. Do not look upon Qaḍā Fakān, and do not come here again from this day on.”
sentences.n: kāna … ḥājatun, “there is a need”: the verb stays masculine before its feminine subject, as often when words come between. lā tanẓur, “do not look”, takes its object directly, as in the spoken language, where Classical prose prefers naẓara ilā. wa-lā ʿudta tarjiʿu, “and may you no more come back”, is spoken Arabic: ʿāda with a following verb means “to do again, any more”, and lā with the perfect makes it a prohibition or a wish. hunā, “here”, for “to here”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَهَا قَامَ وَخَرَجَ وَلَمْ يَنْطِقْ بِحَرْفٍ وَاحِدٍ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى وَالِدَتِهِ أَعْلَمَهَا بِمَا قَالَتْهُ عَمَّتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmahā qāma wa-kharaja wa-lam yanṭiq bi-ḥarfin wāḥidin wa-dakhala ʿalā wālidatihi aʿlamahā bi-mā qālathu ʿammatuhu
sentences.l: And when he heard her speech he rose and went out and did not utter a single letter, and he went in to his mother, he informed her of what his aunt had said.
sentences.i: When he heard her words he rose and went out without uttering a syllable, went in to his mother, and told her what his aunt had said.
sentences.n: aʿlamahā, “he informed her”, follows dakhala with no “and”: two verbs set side by side, as often in the spoken language. naṭaqa bi-, “to utter”; aʿlama bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the thing told. The print marks the doubled mīm of ʿammatuhu (عمّته).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّمَا نَشَأَ هٰذَا مِنْ كَثْرَةِ كَلَامِكَ وَأَنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ حَدِيثَ حُبِّكَ لِقَضَى فَكَانَ شَاعَ وَانْتَشَرَلَهُ ذِكْرٌ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu innamā nashaʾa hādhā min kathrati kalāmika wa-anta taʿlamu anna ḥadītha ḥubbika li-qaḍā fakāna shāʿa wa-intashara lahu dhikrun fī kulli makānin
sentences.l: And she said to him: This only arose from the muchness of your talk; and you know that the tale of your love for Qaḍā Fakān has spread, and there has spread-abroad for it a mention in every place.
sentences.i: She said to him, “This has come only of your talking so much. You know that the story of your love for Qaḍā Fakān has got about, and it is spoken of everywhere.
sentences.n: innamā, “only”, gives the cause as the whole of it. ḥubb … li-, “love for”: li- marks the one loved. The print runs intashara into the next word (وانتشرله), and marks the doubled bāʾ of ḥubbika (حبّك).

sentences.t: وَكَيْفَ أَنْتَ تَأْكُلُ زَادَهُمْ وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَعْشَقُ بِنْتَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-kayfa anta taʾkulu zādahum wa-baʿda dhālika taʿshaqu bintahum
sentences.l: And how (is it that) you eat their provision and after that you love their daughter?
sentences.i: How can you eat their bread and then fall in love with their daughter?
sentences.n: zād, “provisions, food for the road”: to have eaten a man's food binds one to him, and his household's honour becomes one's own charge. ʿashiqa, “to be passionately in love with”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَمَنْ يَأْخُذُهَا غَيْرِي وَهِيَ بِنْتُ عَمِّي وَأَنَا أَحَقُّ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-man yaʾkhudhuhā ghayrī wa-hiya bintu ʿammī wa-anā aḥaqqu bihā
sentences.l: And he said: And who takes her other-than me, when she is the daughter of my uncle, and I am more-entitled to her?
sentences.i: He said, “And who should marry her but me? She is my cousin, and I have the best right to her.”
sentences.n: bint ʿammī, “my paternal uncle's daughter”: by custom a man had the first claim on his father's brother's daughter. akhadha, “to take”, is the plain word for taking a wife. aḥaqqu bi-, “more entitled to”: bi- marks what one has a right to.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أُمُّهُ بَطِّلْ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ وَاسْكُتْ لِئَلَّا يَصِلَ الْخَبَرُ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ فَيَكُونَ ذٰلِكَ سَبَبَ حِرْمَانِكَ مِنْهَا وَسَبَبَ هَلَاكِكَ وَكَثْرَةِ أَحْزَانِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ummuhu baṭṭil hādhā al-kalāma wa-uskut li-allā yaṣila al-khabaru ilā al-maliki sāsāna fa-yakūna dhālika sababa ḥirmānika minhā wa-sababa halākika wa-kathrati aḥzānika
sentences.l: And his mother said to him: Stop this talk, and be silent, lest the news reach al-Malik Sāsān, and that be the cause of your being-deprived of her, and the cause of your perishing and the muchness of your sorrows.
sentences.i: His mother said to him, “Have done with this talk and hold your tongue, lest word of it reach al-Malik Sāsān, and that be the reason you are denied her, and the cause of your ruin and of many sorrows.
sentences.n: baṭṭil, “stop, leave off”, is the spoken imperative of baṭṭala, “to make void”, still the everyday word for “stop it” in Egypt and Syria; the print marks its doubled ṭāʾ, and the doubled mīm of ummuhu (امّه). li-allā, “so that not”, lest. ḥirmān, “deprivation”. More rhyme: ḥirmānika, aḥzānika.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَبْعَثُوا لَنَا فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ عَشَاءً نَأْكُلُهُ وَنَمُوتُ جُوعًا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yabʿathū lanā fī hādhihi al-laylati ʿashāʾan naʾkuluhu wa-namūtu jūʿan
sentences.l: And they have not sent to us on this night a supper we might eat it, and we are dying of hunger.
sentences.i: And tonight they have not sent us any supper to eat, and we are starving.
sentences.n: The widow and her son live on what the palace sends them. jūʿan, “of hunger”: the accusative gives the cause. namūtu jūʿan, “we die of hunger”, is the ordinary overstatement of daily speech.

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ لَوْكُنَّا فِي بَلَدٍ غَيْرِ هٰذِهِ لَكُنَّا هَلَكْنَا مِنْ أَلَمِ الْجُوعِ أَوْ ذُلِّ السُّؤَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu law kunnā fī baladin ghayri hādhihi la-kunnā halaknā min alami al-jūʿi aw dhulli al-suʾāli
sentences.l: And we, if we were in a country other than this, we would have perished from the pain of the hunger or the abasement of the asking.
sentences.i: If we lived in any town but this, we would have perished long ago of the pangs of hunger or the shame of begging.”
sentences.n: The print runs law into kunnā (لوكنا). la-kunnā halaknā, “we would have perished”: kāna with a past verb gives the pluperfect, la- marks the answer to law. suʾāl, “asking”, here asking for alms; dhull al-suʾāl, “the abasement of begging”, is a set phrase. balad is feminine here (hādhihi).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنْ أُمِّهِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ زَادَتْ حَسْرَتُهُ وَدَمَعَتْ عَيْنَيْهِ فَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kāna mā kāna min ummihi hādhā al-kalāma zādat ḥasratuhu wa-damaʿat ʿaynayhi fa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard from his mother this speech, his grief increased and his two eyes shed-tears, and he moaned and complained, and he recited, saying:
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard these words from his mother his grief grew; his eyes filled with tears, and he moaned and lamented and recited:
sentences.n: ʿaynayhi, “his two eyes”, is the subject of damaʿat, where Classical Arabic has ʿaynāhu; spoken Arabic uses the -ayn form of the dual for every case, and the text follows it. anna, “to moan, groan”; the print marks its doubled nūn (فانّ). ḥasra, “sorrow, grief for what is lost”.

sentences.t:
اَقِلِّي مِنَ اللَّوْمِ الَّذِي لَا يُفَارِقُ * فَقَلْبِي اِلىَ مَنْ تَيَّمَتْهُ لَعَاشِقُ
وَلَا تَطْلُبِي عِنْدِي مِنَ الصَّبْرِ ذَرَّةً * فَصَبْرِي وَبَيْتِ اللّٰهِ مِنِّي طَالِقُ
اِذَا سَامَنِي اللُّوَّامُ نَهْيًا عَصَيْتُهُمْ * وَهَا اَنَا فِي دَعْوَى الْمَحَبَّةِ صَادِقُ
وَقَدْ مَنَعُونِي عَنْوَةً اَنْ اَزُورَهَا * وَهَا اَنَا وَالرَّحْمٰنِ مَا اَنَا فَاسِقُ
وَاِنَّ عِظَامِي حِينَ تَسْمَعُ ذِكْرَهَا * تُشَابِهُ طَيْرًا خَلْفَهُنَّ بَوَاشِقُ
اَلَا قُلْ لِمَنْ قَدْ لَامَ فِي الْحُبِّ اِنَّنِي * لِوَجْهِكَ حَقًّا بِنْتَ عَمِّي لَعَاشِقُ
sentences.tr:
aqillī mina al-lawmi alladhī lā yufāriqu * fa-qalbī ilā man tayyamathu la-ʿāshiqu
wa-lā taṭlubī ʿindī mina al-ṣabri dharratan * fa-ṣabrī wa-bayti allāhi minnī ṭāliqu
idhā sāmanī al-luwwāmu nahyan ʿaṣaytuhum * wa-hā anā fī daʿwā al-maḥabbati ṣādiqu
wa-qad manaʿūnī ʿanwatan an azūrahā * wa-hā anā wa-al-raḥmāni mā anā fāsiqu
wa-inna ʿiẓāmī ḥīna tasmaʿu dhikrahā * tushābihu ṭayran khalfahunna bawāshiqu
alā qul li-man qad lāma fī al-ḥubbi innanī * li-wajhika ḥaqqan binta ʿammī la-ʿāshiqu
sentences.l:
Lessen of the blame which does not leave-off, * for my heart, toward her who has enslaved it, is indeed a lover;
and do not seek with me of the patience a grain, * for my patience — by the House of God — is from me divorced.
When the blamers impose on me a forbidding, I disobey them, * and here I am, in the claim of the love truthful.
And they have prevented me by force that I visit her, * and here I am — by the Merciful — I am not a transgressor.
And truly my bones, when they hear the mention of her, * resemble birds behind which (are) sparrowhawks.
Ah, say to whoever has blamed in the love: truly I, * for your face, truly, daughter of my uncle, am indeed a lover.
sentences.i:
Spare me the blame that never leaves off, * for my heart is in love with her who has enslaved it.
Do not look to me for one grain of patience: * by the House of God, my patience and I are divorced.
When the censurers lay their bans on me, I defy them, * and here I stand, true in my claim of love.
They have kept me by force from visiting her, * yet, by the Merciful, I am no sinner.
Whenever my bones hear her named, they are * like birds with the hawks behind them.
Say to him who blames me for love: in truth, * O daughter of my uncle, it is your face I love.
sentences.n: Six lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -iqu, copied as the print points them. aqillī, “lessen”, is a feminine imperative: he speaks to his mother. tayyama, of love, “to enslave, make abject”; the subject is she, the cousin. ṭāliq, “divorced”, is the word for a wife put away; he swears “by the House of God”, the Kaʿba, that his patience has left him for good. lāʾim, plural luwwām, “blamer(s)”, the stock censurers of love poetry; sāma, “to impose a hard thing on someone”. fāsiq, “transgressor, libertine”. bawāshiq, plural of bāshiq, a small hawk (the sparrowhawk): his bones tremble like small birds with hawks on their tails. In the last line he turns to the cousin herself; the print points li-wajhika with the masculine “your”, though binta ʿammī, “daughter of my uncle”, is a woman, perhaps for the metre's sake or by a slip of the pointing.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ لِأُمِّهِ مَا بَقِيَ لِي عِنْدَ عَمَّتِي وَلَا عِنْدَ هٰؤُلَاءِ الْقَوْمِ مَقَامٌ بَلْ أَخْرُجُ مِنَ الْقَصْرِ وَأَسْكُنُ فِي أَطْرَافِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla li-ummihi mā baqiya lī ʿinda ʿammatī wa-lā ʿinda hāʾulāʾi al-qawmi maqāmun bal akhruju mina al-qaṣri wa-askunu fī aṭrāfi al-madīnati
sentences.l: And when he finished from his poetry, he said to his mother: There remains not for me with my aunt, nor with these people, a staying-place; rather I will go out from the palace and dwell in the edges of the city.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he said to his mother, “There is no place left for me with my aunt, or with these people. I will leave the palace and live on the outskirts of the city.”
sentences.n: ʿammatī, “my aunt”: Nuzhat al-Zamān, in whose palace he has been living. maqām, “a place to stay”. aṭrāf al-madīna, “the extremities of the city”, its outlying quarters. The print marks the doubled mīm of ʿammatī.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَتْ بِهِ أُمُّهُ مِنَ الْقَصْرِ وَجَاؤُا بِجِوَارِ قَوْمٍ صَعَالِيكَ وَسَكَنُوا
sentences.tr: fa-kharajat bihi ummuhu mina al-qaṣri wa-jāʾū bi-jiwāri qawmin ṣaʿālīka wa-sakanū
sentences.l: So his mother went out with him from the palace, and they came to the neighbourhood of a people, paupers, and dwelt.
sentences.i: So his mother left the palace with him, and they came to live among poor folk, and settled there.
sentences.n: kharaja bi-, “to go out with, take out”: bi- marks the one taken along. jāʾū … wa-sakanū, “they came … and settled”, are plural for two people, as the spoken language has it; the print spells jāʾū with its hamza on the wāw and a single wāw (جاؤا). bi-jiwāri, “in the neighbourhood of”. ṣaʿālīk, plural of ṣuʿlūk, “a pauper, a vagabond”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَتْ أُمُّهُ تَتَرَدَّدُ إِلَى قَصْرِ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ وَتَأْخُذُ مِنْهُ مَا تَقْتَاتُ بِهِ هِيَ وَإِيَّاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārat ummuhu tataraddadu ilā qaṣri al-maliki sāsāna wa-taʾkhudhu minhu mā taqtātu bihi hiya wa-iyyāhu
sentences.l: And his mother began to go-back-and-forth to the palace of al-Malik Sāsān and to take from it what she would feed-herself with, she and him.
sentences.i: His mother would come and go to the palace of al-Malik Sāsān and take from it what she needed to feed herself and her son.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “she took to …”. taraddada ilā, “to keep going to, frequent”. al-Malik Sāsān, “King Sāsān”, is the Great Chamberlain under his throne name. iqtāta bi-, “to feed oneself on”: bi- marks the food. hiya wa-iyyāhu, “she and him”: the object pronoun iyyāhu stands where Classical would have huwa, “he”, a turn of the spoken language.

sentences.t: هٰذَا ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَضَى فَكَانَ اخْتَلَتْ بِأُمِّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا عَمَّتَاهْ كَيْفَ حَالُ وَلَدِكِ
sentences.tr: hādhā thumma inna qaḍā fakāna ikhtalat bi-ummi kāna mā kāna wa-qālat lahā yā ʿammatāh kayfa ḥālu waladiki
sentences.l: This; then Qaḍā Fakān was-alone with the mother of Kān Mā Kān and said to her: O my aunt, how is the state of your son?
sentences.i: So it was. Then Qaḍā Fakān took Kān Mā Kān's mother aside and said to her, “Aunt, how is your son?”
sentences.n: hādhā, “this (is how it was)”, closes the scene. ikhtalā bi-, “to be alone with, take aside”: bi- marks the one she is alone with. yā ʿammatāh, “O aunt!”, with the lengthened -āh of a heartfelt call; the print marks the doubled mīm. A ʿamma is properly a father's sister; she gives the name to her uncle's widow out of affection and respect.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَا بِنْتِي آهْ بَاكِي الْعَيْنِ حَزِينُ الْقَلْبِ وَاقِعٌ فِي شَرَكِ هَوَاكِ وَأَنْشَدَتْهَا مَا قَالَهُ مِنَ الْأَبْيَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā bintī āh bākī al-ʿayni ḥazīnu al-qalbi wāqiʿun fī sharaki hawāki wa-anshadathā mā qālahu mina al-abyāti
sentences.l: And she said: O my daughter, ah! weeping of the eye, sad of the heart, fallen into the snare of the love of you. And she recited to her what he had said of the lines.
sentences.i: “Ah, my daughter,” she said, “his eyes weep, his heart is sad, he is caught in the snare of his love for you.” And she recited to her the lines he had spoken.
sentences.n: The print has اه, read here as the sigh āh, “ah!”; it may instead be a slip for innahu, “he is …”, which gives the same sense with the description that follows. bākī al-ʿayn, ḥazīn al-qalb, “weeping of eye, sad of heart”: an adjective with the part of the body it applies to. sharak, “snare, net”. hawāki, “your love”, here the love felt for you. anshada takes two objects, the hearer and the poem: the lines are the ones he has just spoken.

sentences.t: فَبَكَتْ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَقَالَتْ وَاللّٰهِ مَا هَجَرْتُهُ لِكَلَامِهِ وَلَا بُغْضًا لَهُ وَلٰكِنْ خَوْفًا عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْأَعْدَاءِ وَإِنَّ عِنْدِي مِنَ الشَّوْقِ لَهُ أَضْعَافَ مَا عِنْدَهُ لِي وَلَا يَقْدِرُ لِسَانِي عَلَى وَصْفِ شَوْقِي لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-bakat qaḍā fakāna wa-qālat wa-allāhi mā hajartuhu li-kalāmihi wa-lā bughḍan lahu wa-lākin khawfan ʿalayhi mina al-aʿdāʾi wa-inna ʿindī mina al-shawqi lahu aḍʿāfa mā ʿindahu lī wa-lā yaqdiru lisānī ʿalā waṣfi shawqī lahu
sentences.l: And Qaḍā Fakān wept and said: By God, I did not shun him for his speech, nor in hatred of him, but in fear for him from the enemies; and with me of the longing for him are multiples of what is with him for me, and my tongue is not able to describe my longing for him.
sentences.i: Qaḍā Fakān wept and said, “By God, I did not turn from him for what he said, nor because I hate him, but out of fear for him from his enemies. I long for him many times more than he longs for me, and my tongue cannot describe my longing for him.
sentences.n: bughḍan and khawfan are accusatives of reason: “out of hatred”, “out of fear”. khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for”: ʿalā marks the one in danger, min the danger. inna ʿindī … aḍʿāfa, “there are with me … multiples”: the subject of inna, aḍʿāf, “doubles, many times over”, comes after the fronted ʿindī. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا عَثَرَاتُ لِسَانِهِ وَخَفَقَانُ جَنَانِهِ مَا قَطَعَ أَبِي عَنْهُ إِحْسَانَهُ وَأَوْلَاةُ مَنْعَهُ وَحِرْمَانَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā ʿatharātu lisānihi wa-khafaqānu janānihi mā qaṭaʿa abī ʿanhu iḥsānahu wa-awlāhu manʿahu wa-ḥirmānahu
sentences.l: And were it not for the stumblings of his tongue and the fluttering of his heart, my father would not have cut off from him his kindness and dealt him his withholding and his depriving.
sentences.i: Had his tongue not run away with him and his heart not fluttered so, my father would never have cut off his bounty from him, nor dealt him refusal and want.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: lisānihi, janānihi, iḥsānahu, ḥirmānahu. abī, “my father”, is the Chamberlain, now al-Malik Sāsān, who has brought her up; her own father was Sharrukān. The print writes the pronoun of awlāhu with tāʾ marbūṭa (واولاة), the two endings being often confused; it is read awlāhu, from awlā, “to make (something) someone's portion”, with two objects.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنَّ أَيَّامَ الْوَرَى دُوَلٌ وَالصَّبْرُ فِي كُلِّ الْأُمُورِ أَجْمَلُ وَلَعَلَّ مَنْ قَضَى عَلَيْنَا بِالْفِرَاقِ أَنْ يَمُنَّ لَنَا بِالتَّلَاقِ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinna ayyāma al-warā duwalun wa-al-ṣabru fī kulli al-umūri ajmalu wa-laʿalla man qaḍā ʿalaynā bi-al-firāqi an yamunna lanā bi-al-talāqi thumma anshadat taqūlu hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: But the days of mankind are turns, and the patience in all the matters is most-beautiful; and perhaps He who decreed against us the parting will grant to us the meeting. Then she recited, saying these two lines:
sentences.i: But the days of men go round by turns, and in all things patience is the fairest course. Perhaps He who decreed our parting will grant us to meet again.” Then she recited these two lines:
sentences.n: duwal, plural of dawla, “a turn (of fortune)”: fortune passes from hand to hand. al-ṣabru ajmal, “patience is fairer”, recalls the Qurʾān's ṣabrun jamīl, “a fair patience” (12:84). Rhyme: firāq, talāq; talāq is a verbal noun of talāqā, “to meet one another”, in the form the Qurʾān uses (40:15). qaḍā ʿalā … bi-, “to decree (something) against someone”, the verb of her own name, Qaḍā. manna bi-, “to bestow as a favour”, usually takes ʿalā for the one favoured, here li-; the print marks the doubled nūn. laʿalla is followed by an and a verb, “perhaps that …”, a looser construction than the Classical one.

sentences.t:
اَيَا بْنَ الْعَمِّ عِنْدِيْ مِنْ غَرَامِيْ * كَامْثَالِ الَّذِيْ قَدْ حَلَّ عِنْدَكْ
وَلٰكِنِّيْ كَتَمْتُ النَّاسَ وَجْدِيْ * فَهَلَّا كُنْتَ اَنْتَ كَتَمْتَ وَجْدَكْ
sentences.tr:
ayā bna al-ʿammi ʿindī min gharāmī * ka-amthāli alladhī qad ḥalla ʿindak
wa-lākinnī katamtu al-nāsa wajdī * fa-hallā kunta anta katamta wajdak
sentences.l:
O son of the uncle, with me of my passion * like the likes of what has alighted with you;
but I hid from the people my longing: * so why were you not, you, hiding your longing?
sentences.i:
Cousin, there dwells in me a passion * the equal of the one that dwells in you;
but I have kept my longing from the world: * why could you not have kept yours hidden too?
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre wāfir, rhyming in -dak, copied as the print points them. ibn al-ʿamm, “son of the paternal uncle”, cousin; ayā is a call, “O”, and the alif of ibn falls away after it (ayā bna). ka-amthāli, “like the likes of”, doubles the comparison. ḥalla, “to alight, take up lodging”. katama, “to hide”, here with two objects: the people and the longing. hallā, “why not”, reproaches a thing left undone. The rhyme words end in a pausal -dak, which the print marks with sukūn.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنْهَا أُمُّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ ذٰلِكَ شَكَرَتْهَا وَدَعَتْ لَهَا وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَأَعْلَمَتْ وَلَدَهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ بِذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat minhā ummu kāna mā kāna dhālika shakarathā wa-daʿat lahā wa-kharajat min ʿindihā wa-aʿlamat waladahā kāna mā kāna bi-dhālika
sentences.l: And when the mother of Kān Mā Kān heard that from her, she thanked her and prayed for her and went out from her presence, and informed her son Kān Mā Kān of that.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān's mother heard this from her, she thanked her, called down blessings on her and left her, and told her son Kān Mā Kān all of it.
sentences.n: daʿā li-, “to pray for”; daʿā ʿalā is “to pray against, curse”. aʿlama bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the thing told.

sentences.t: فَزَادَ طَمَعُهُ فِيهَا وَقَوِيَتْ نَفْسُهُ بَعْدَ أَنْ كَانَ قَطَعَ يَأْسَهُ وَخَمَدَتْ أَنْفَاسُهُ وَقَالَ وَاللّٰهِ مَا أُرِيدُ سِوَاهَا وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-zāda ṭamaʿuhu fīhā wa-qawiyat nafsuhu baʿda an kāna qaṭaʿa yaʾsahu wa-khamadat anfāsuhu wa-qāla wa-allāhi mā urīdu siwāhā wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And his hope in her increased, and his soul grew-strong, after he had cut off his despair and his breaths had died down; and he said: By God, I do not want other than her. And he recited, saying: Poetry.
sentences.i: His hope of her grew and his spirit revived, though he had given up all hope and his very breath had sunk low. “By God,” he said, “I want no one but her,” and he recited:
sentences.n: ṭamaʿ fī, “hope, desire for”. qaṭaʿa yaʾsahu, “he had cut off his despair”, is a strange phrase, and it is not certain how to take it; the sense wanted is that he had given up hope, and it may blend qaṭaʿa rajāʾahu, “he cut off his hope”, with yaʾisa, “he despaired”. The print writes yaʾs without its hamza (ياسه). khamadat anfāsuhu, “his breaths had died down”, as a fire goes out. shiʿr, “poetry”, standing alone after yaqūlu, is the print's heading to the verses that follow.

sentences.t:
دِع اللَّوْمَ لَا اَصْغِيْ اِلى قَوْلِ لَائِمِ * فَقَدْ بُحْتُ بِالسِّرِّ الَّذِيْ كُنْتُ كَاتِمَا
وَقَدْ غَابَ عَنِّيْ مَنْ اُرَجِّيْ وِصَالَهُ * وَقَدْ سَهَرَتْ عَيْنِيْ وَقَدْ بَاتَ نَائِمَا
sentences.tr:
diʿi al-lawma lā aṣghī ilā qawli lāʾimi * fa-qad buḥtu bi-al-sirri alladhī kuntu kātimā
wa-qad ghāba ʿannī man urajjī wiṣālahu * wa-qad saharat ʿaynī wa-qad bāta nāʾimā
sentences.l:
Leave the blame! I do not listen to the saying of a blamer, * for I have disclosed the secret that I was hiding;
and he has gone-away from me whose union I hope for, * and my eye has stayed-awake while he has passed-the-night sleeping.
sentences.i:
Leave off your blame: I will not heed the blamer, * for I have told the secret I once kept;
the one whose love I hope for is far from me, * and my eye lies awake while that one sleeps.
sentences.n: Two lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -imā, copied as the print points them. The print sets a kasra under the first letter (دِع); the imperative of wadaʿa, “to leave”, is daʿ (daʿi before the article), and the sense is not in doubt. aṣghī, printed with a fatḥa, stands for uṣghī, “I listen”, from aṣghā ilā. saharat is printed with a fatḥa on the hāʾ for sahirat, “stayed awake”. bāḥa bi-, “to disclose”. The beloved is spoken of as masculine (wiṣālahu, bāta), the usual convention of love poetry. In kātimā, nāʾimā the rhyme lengthens the final vowel.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَضَتِ الْأَيَّامُ وَاللَّيَالِي وَهُوَ يَتَقَلَّبُ عَلَى جَمْرِ الْمَقَالِي حَتَّى مَضَي لَهُ مِنَ الْعُمْرِ سَبْعَةَ عَشَرَ سَنَهْ وَقَدْ كَمُلَ حُسْنُهُ وَتَمَّ ظَرْفُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma maḍati al-ayyāmu wa-al-layālī wa-huwa yataqallabu ʿalā jamri al-maqālī ḥattā maḍā lahu mina al-ʿumri sabʿata ʿashara sanah wa-qad kamula ḥusnuhu wa-tamma ẓarfuhu
sentences.l: Then the days and the nights passed, and he turning-over upon the embers of the frying-pans, until there passed for him of age seventeen year; and his beauty had become-complete and his grace was perfected.
sentences.i: So the days and nights went by while he tossed as if on the coals beneath a frying pan, until he reached the age of seventeen, his beauty full grown and his grace complete.
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-layālī, al-maqālī. To “turn over on the embers of the frying pans” (maqālī, plural of miqlāh) is a stock image of restless torment. The print spells maḍā with a yāʾ (مضي), its habit with this verb, and the age is in Middle Arabic: sabʿata ʿashara sanah, where Classical would say sabʿa ʿashrata sanatan, with the numeral agreeing and the counted noun in the accusative. The ending of sana is written ه, read pausally. kamula and tamma, “became complete”, are a near-synonymous pair: ẓarf is grace and elegance of manner. The print marks the doubled lām of yataqallabu and the doubled mīm of tamma.

sentences.t: فَسَهِرَ لَيْلَةً مِنَ اللَّيَالِي وَحَدَّثَ نَفْسَهُ وَقَالَ مَالِي أَسْكُتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي حَتَّى أَذُوبَ وَلَا أَرَى حَبِيبِي وَمَالِي عَيْبٌ إِلَّا الْفَقْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-sahira laylatan mina al-layālī wa-ḥaddatha nafsahu wa-qāla mā lī askutu ʿalā nafsī ḥattā adhūba wa-lā arā ḥabībī wa-mā lī ʿaybun illā al-faqru
sentences.l: And he lay-awake a night of the nights, and spoke-to his soul, and said: What is (it) to me (that) I keep silent upon myself until I melt and do not see my beloved? And I have no fault except the poverty.
sentences.i: One night he lay awake and reasoned with himself, saying, “Why should I hold my peace until I waste away, and never see my beloved? I have no fault but my poverty.
sentences.n: mā lī …, “what is wrong with me that …?”, set as one word (مالي), as the print often runs ما and لي together; in wa-mā lī ʿaybun the same letters mean “I have no fault”. ḥaddatha nafsahu, “to talk to oneself”. sakata ʿalā nafsihi, “to keep silent over one's own trouble”. dhāba, “to melt”, here to waste away with love.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَرْحَلَ مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْبِلَادِ وَأَشِتَّ فِى الْبَرَارِي وَالْقِفَارِ فَإِنَّ مُقَامِي فِي هٰذِهِ الْبِلَادِ عَذَابٌ وَلَالِي فِيهَا صَدِيقٌ وَلَا حَبِيبٌ يُسَلِّينِي
sentences.tr: wa-allāhi innī urīdu an arḥala min hādhihi al-bilādi wa-ashitta fī al-barārī wa-al-qifāri fa-inna muqāmī fī hādhihi al-bilādi ʿadhābun wa-lā lī fīhā ṣadīqun wa-lā ḥabībun yusallīnī
sentences.l: And by God, I want to depart from this country and to scatter-away in the wildernesses and the wastes; for my staying in this country (is) torment, and not to-me in it a friend nor a beloved (who) consoles me.
sentences.i: By God, I mean to leave this land and wander off into the deserts and the wastelands, for to stay here is torment: I have no friend in it, and no loved one to console me.
sentences.n: shatta, “to be scattered, to stray far”; the print marks the doubled tāʾ. barārī and qifār, “open deserts” and “waterless wastes”, a stock pair. The print runs lā and lī together (ولالي), read wa-lā lī, “and I have not”. sallā, “to console, divert”.

sentences.t: وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أُسَلِّيَ نَفْسِي بِالْغُرْبَةِ عَنِ الْوَطَنِ حَتَّى أَمُوتَ وَأَسْتَرِيحَ مِنْ هٰذَا الذُّلِّ وَالْمِحَنِ
sentences.tr: wa-urīdu an usalliya nafsī bi-al-ghurbati ʿani al-waṭani ḥattā amūta wa-astarīḥa min hādhā al-dhulli wa-al-miḥani
sentences.l: And I want to console my soul with the estrangement from the homeland, until I die and rest from this abasement and the trials.”
sentences.i: I would rather console myself with exile from home until I die and find rest from this humiliation and these trials.”
sentences.n: ghurba, “being a stranger”, exile far from one's own land: bi- marks the means of consolation. Rhyme: al-waṭani, al-miḥani (miḥan, plural of miḥna, “trial, affliction”).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَنْشَدَ وَجَعَلَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu anshada wa-jaʿala yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then he recited and began saying these verses — poetry:
sentences.i: Then he began to recite these verses:
sentences.n: jaʿala yaqūlu, “he set about saying”: jaʿala with a following verb marks the start of an action. shiʿr, “poetry”, is the print's heading for the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
دَعْ مُهْجَتِيْ تَزْدَادُ فِيْ خَفَقَانِهَا * لَيْسَ التَّذَلُّلُ فِى الْعِدَى مِنْ شَانِهَا
وَاعْذُرْ فَاِنَّ حُشَاشَتِيْ كَصَحِيْفَةٍ * لَا شَكَّ اَنَّ الدَّمْعَ مِنْ عُنْوَانِهَا
هَا بِنْتَ عَمِّيْ قَدْ بَدَتْ حُوْرِيَّةً * نَزَلَتْ اِلَيْنَا عَنْ رِضَى رِضْوَانِهَا
مَنْ رَامَ اَلْحَاظَ الْعُيُونِ مُعَارِضًا * لِسُيُوفِهَا لَمْ يَنْجُ مِنْ عُدْوَانِهَا
sentences.tr:
daʿ muhjatī tazdādu fī khafaqānihā * laysa al-tadhallulu fī al-ʿidā min shānihā
wa-iʿdhur fa-inna ḥushāshatī ka-ṣaḥīfatin * lā shakka anna al-damʿa min ʿunwānihā
hā binta ʿammī qad badat ḥūriyyatan * nazalat ilaynā ʿan riḍā riḍwānihā
man rāma alḥāẓa al-ʿuyūni muʿāriḍan * li-suyūfihā lam yanju min ʿudwānihā
sentences.l:
Let my heart-blood increase in its throbbing; * abasement among the enemies is not of its manner.
And excuse (me), for my last-breath of life is like a page; * no doubt the tears are of its superscription.
Lo, the daughter of my uncle has appeared, a houri * who came down to us with the consent of her Riḍwān.
Whoever seeks the glances of the eyes, opposing * their swords, does not escape from their aggression.
sentences.i:
Let my heart beat ever harder; * to grovel before enemies is not its way.
Forgive me: what life is left in me is a letter * and, beyond doubt, its tears are the address upon it.
See, my cousin has appeared, a houri * come down to us with the leave of Paradise's keeper.
Whoever sets himself against the swords * of those glancing eyes will not escape their violence.
sentences.n: A poem in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -ānihā, copied as the print points it. muhja, “heart's blood”, the soul itself. The print writes shān for shaʾn, “manner, concern”, without hamza. ḥushāsha is the last breath of life in a body; ʿunwān, the address written on the outside of a letter, so the tears announce what is inside. hā, “lo, here is”. Riḍwān is the angel who keeps the gate of Paradise; the houris are its maidens, and riḍā, “consent”, puns on his name. alḥāẓ, “glances”, plural of laḥẓ, are the swords of the beloved's eyes.

sentences.t:
سَاسِيْرُ اَرْضَ اللّٰهِ غَيْرَ مُقَصِّرِ * كَيْ اَنْ اَنَالَ الرِّزْقَ مِنْ حِرْمَانِهَا
سَاسِيْرُ فِي الْاَرْضِ الْوَسِيعَةِ مُنْقِذًا * نَفْسِي وَاَمْنَحُهَا سِوَى حِرْمَانِهَا
وَاَعُودُ مَسْرُورَ الْفُؤادِ مُنَعَّمًا * وَاُقَاتِلُ الْاَبْطَالَ فِي مَيْدَانِهَا
وَلَسَوْفَ اَشْتَاقُ الْغَنَائِمَ عَائِدًا * وَاَصُولُ مُقْتَدِرًا عَلى اَقْرَانِهَا
sentences.tr:
sa-asīru arḍa allāhi ghayra muqaṣṣiri * kay an anāla al-rizqa min ḥirmānihā
sa-asīru fī al-arḍi al-wasīʿati munqidhan * nafsī wa-amnaḥuhā siwā ḥirmānihā
wa-aʿūdu masrūra al-fuʾādi munaʿʿaman * wa-uqātilu al-abṭāla fī maydānihā
wa-la-sawfa ashtāqu al-ghanāʾima ʿāʾidan * wa-aṣūlu muqtadiran ʿalā aqrānihā
sentences.l:
I shall journey (through) the land of God, not falling-short, * so that I may obtain the provision from its withholding.
I shall journey in the wide land, rescuing * my soul, and I shall grant it other than its deprivation.
And I shall return glad of heart, made-to-live-in-ease, * and I shall fight the champions in its field.
And surely I shall long for the spoils, returning, * and I shall assault, empowered, over its peers.
sentences.i:
I will travel God's earth and not hold back, * to wring my living from what it denies me.
I will travel the wide earth to save * myself, and give my soul more than want.
Then I will come home glad of heart and prosperous, * and fight the champions on their field.
And I will crave the spoils as I return, * and charge in strength against my equals.
sentences.n: The same poem continues. The print writes sa-asīru with a bare alif and no hamza. kay an, “so that”, doubles the particle of purpose, a common post-classical turn. The rhyme word ḥirmānihā, “its withholding”, is used twice running. aqrān, plural of qirn, “a match in battle”, the man of one's own mettle. The last line is loosely put: the sense seems to be that he will come back hungry for plunder and strong against all rivals.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْقَصْرِ حَافِيًا مَاشِيًا فِي قَمِيصٍ قَصِيرِ الْأَكْمَامِ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهِ لِبْدَةٌ لَهَا سَبْعَةُ أَعْوَامٍ وَصُحْبَتَهُ رَغِيفٌ نَاشِفٌ لَهُ ثَلٰثَهُ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna kāna mā kāna kharaja mina al-qaṣri ḥāfiyan māshiyan fī qamīṣin qaṣīri al-akmāmi wa-ʿalā raʾsihi libdatun lahā sabʿatu aʿwāmin wa-ṣuḥbatahu raghīfun nāshifun lahu thalāthatu ayyāmin
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān went out from the palace barefoot, walking, in a shirt short of the sleeves, and on his head a felt-cap that had seven years, and in-his-company a loaf dry that had three days.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān left the palace on foot and barefoot, in a short-sleeved shirt, with a felt cap seven years old on his head and a dry loaf three days old for company.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: akmām, aʿwām, ayyām, and ẓalām in the next sentence. libda, a skullcap of felt, the poor man's headgear. ṣuḥbatahu, “in his company”, is used here as a preposition, “with him”. nāshif, “dry”, is the colloquial word (Classical yābis). The print spells thalātha “three” defectively, with the small alif over the lām, and ends it in hāʾ for tāʾ marbūṭa (ثلٰثه).

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَ فِي حِنْدِسِ الظَّلَامِ وَأَتَي إِلَى بَابِ الْأَزَجِ بِبَغْدَادَ فَوَقَفَ هُنَاكَ
sentences.tr: wa-kharaja fī ḥindisi al-ẓalāmi wa-atā ilā bābi al-azaji bi-baghdāda fa-waqafa hunāka
sentences.l: And he went out in the pitch of the darkness, and came to the Gate of al-Azaj in Baghdad, and stood there.
sentences.i: He went out in the black of night, came to the Azaj Gate of Baghdad, and waited there.
sentences.n: The print has الارج, a misprint for الازج, corrected here. Bāb al-Azaj, the gate of the Azaj quarter on the east side of Baghdad. ḥindis, “the deepest darkness of night”. The print writes atā with a dotted yāʾ (اتي).

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا فُتِحَ بَابُ الْمَدِينَةِ كَانَ أَوَّلَ مَنْ خَرَجَ مِنْهُ كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَسَاحَ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ فِى الْقِفَارِ لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا
sentences.tr: wa-lammā futiḥa bābu al-madīnati kāna awwala man kharaja minhu kāna mā kāna wa-sāḥa ʿalā wajhihi fī al-qifāri laylan wa-nahāran
sentences.l: And when the gate of the city was opened, the first of whoever went out from it was Kān Mā Kān; and he roamed on his face in the wastes night and day.
sentences.i: When the city gate was opened, Kān Mā Kān was the first to pass out through it, and he wandered where his feet took him through the wilderness, night and day.
sentences.n: kāna awwala man kharaja … kāna mā kāna, “the first who went out was Kān Mā Kān”: the verb kāna and the hero's name, itself made of kāna, stand side by side, and the print runs the name together here (ماكان). sāḥa ʿalā wajhihi, “to roam on his face”, to wander aimlessly, going wherever one's face is turned. qifār, plural of qafr, “empty desert”.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا أَتَى اللَّيْلُ طَلَبَتْهُ أُمُّهُ فَلَمْ تَجِدْهُ أَبَدًا فَضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهَا الدُّنْيَا بِاتِّسَاعِهَا وَلَمْ تَلْتَذَّ بِشَيْءٍ مِنْ مَتَاعِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lammā atā al-laylu ṭalabathu ummuhu fa-lam tajidhu abadan fa-ḍāqat ʿalayhā al-dunyā bi-ittisāʿihā wa-lam taltadhdha bi-shayʾin min matāʿihā
sentences.l: And when the night came, his mother sought him, and she did not find him at all; so the world became narrow upon her with its wideness, and she did not take-delight in a thing of its goods.
sentences.i: When night came his mother looked for him and could not find him anywhere. The world, for all its breadth, closed in on her, and nothing in it gave her any pleasure.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ittisāʿihā, matāʿihā. ḍāqat ʿalayhā al-dunyā bi-ittisāʿihā, “the world grew narrow on her for all its width”, echoes the Qurʾān's ḍāqat ʿalayhim al-arḍu bi-mā raḥubat (9:118). abadan, “ever”, after a negative: “not at all”. iltadhdha bi-, “to take pleasure in”: bi- marks the thing enjoyed. matāʿ, “goods, enjoyments”: what the world has to offer.

sentences.t: فَانْتَظَرَتْهُ أَوَّلَ يَوْمٍ وَثَانِيَ يَوْمٍ وَثَالِثَ يَوْمٍ إِلَى أَنْ مَضَى عَشَرَةُ أَيَّامٍ فَلَمْ تَقَعْ لَهُ عَلَى خَبَرٍ فَضَاقَ صَدْرُهَا وَصَرَخَتْ وَعَيَّطَتْ وَقَالَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-intaẓarathu awwala yawmin wa-thāniya yawmin wa-thālitha yawmin ilā an maḍā ʿasharatu ayyāmin fa-lam taqaʿ lahu ʿalā khabarin fa-ḍāqa ṣadruhā wa-ṣarakhat wa-ʿayyaṭat wa-qālat
sentences.l: And she waited for him the first day, and the second day, and the third day, until ten days passed; and she did not fall for him upon news; so her breast became narrow, and she screamed, and she cried-aloud, and she said:
sentences.i: She waited for him one day, a second and a third, until ten days had gone by, and still she came upon no word of him. Then her heart failed her; she screamed and wailed aloud, and said:
sentences.n: waqaʿa ʿalā khabar, “to fall upon news”, to come across word of someone; lahu, “of him”. maḍā, masculine, with ʿasharatu ayyāmin, “ten days”: the verb often stays masculine before a plural subject. ʿayyaṭa, “to cry out, wail”, is a colloquial word (Egyptian and Syrian ʿayyaṭ, “to shout, weep aloud”); the Classical language has ʿiyāṭ, “shouting”.

sentences.t: يَا وَلَدِى يَا أَنِيسِي هَيَّجْتَ أَحْزَانِي لَقَدْ كَانَ بِي مَاكَفَانِي حَتَّى بَعُدْتَ عَنْ أَوْطَانِي
sentences.tr: yā waladī yā anīsī hayyajta aḥzānī laqad kāna bī mā kafānī ḥattā baʿudta ʿan awṭānī
sentences.l: O my son, O my companion, you have stirred-up my sorrows! There was already in me what was-enough for me, until you went-far from my homelands.
sentences.i: “My son, my dear companion, you have stirred up all my sorrows! I had grief enough already, and now you are gone far from my country.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: aḥzānī, kafānī, awṭānī. anīs, “companion, one whose presence comforts”. The print marks the doubled yāʾ of hayyajta and runs mā kafānī together (ماكفاني). baʿudta could also be read baʿudtu, “until I went far from my homelands”, of her own sorrows; “you went far” suits a son who has vanished better.

sentences.t: فَلَا أُرِيدُ بَعْدَكَ بِطَعَامٍ وَلَا أَلْتَذُّ بِمَنَامٍ وَمَا بَقِيَ لِي إِلَّا الْبُكَاءُ وَالْأَحْزَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-lā urīdu baʿdaka bi-ṭaʿāmin wa-lā altadhdhu bi-manāmin wa-mā baqiya lī illā al-bukāʾu wa-al-aḥzānu
sentences.l: So I do not want after you with food, nor do I take-delight in sleep, and there has not remained for me except the weeping and the sorrows.
sentences.i: Now that you are gone I want no food and take no pleasure in sleep; nothing is left me but weeping and grief.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ṭaʿām, manām. urīdu bi-ṭaʿāmin, “I want with food”: arāda normally takes its object directly, and the bi- has crept in from the parallel altadhdhu bi-, “I take pleasure in”. baʿdaka, “after you”, here “now that you are gone”.

sentences.t: يَا وَلَدِى مِنْ أَيِّ الْبِلَادِ أُنَادِيكَ وَأَيُّ بَلَدٍ تَأْوِيكَ
sentences.tr: yā waladī min ayyi al-bilādi unādīka wa-ayyu baladin taʾwīka
sentences.l: O my son, from which of the lands shall I call you, and which land shelters you?
sentences.i: My son, from what country am I to call you, and what land gives you shelter?”
sentences.n: Rhyme: unādīka, taʾwīka. The print writes taʾwīka without its hamza (تاويك). In Classical usage awā (yaʾwī) means “to take shelter” and āwā (yuʾwī) “to give shelter”; the text uses the first form in the second sense, as later Arabic often does.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَعَّدَتِ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣaʿʿadati al-zafarāti wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then she sent-up the sighs, and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: Then she heaved deep sighs and recited these lines:
sentences.n: ṣaʿʿada, “to make rise”: she sent up sighs from her breast. zafra, a deep sigh drawn up from the chest.

sentences.t:
عَلِمْنَا بِاَنَّا بَعْدَ غَيْبَتِكُمْ نُبْلَى * وَمَدَّتْ قُسِيٌّ لِلْفِرَاقِ لَنَا نَبْلًا
وَقَدْ خَلَّفُونِي بَعْدَ شَدِّ رِحَالِهِمْ * اُعَالِجُ كُربَ الْمَوْتِ اِذْ قَطَعُوا الرَّمْلَا
لَقَدْ هَتَفَتْ بِي جُنْحَ لَيْلٍ حَمَامَةٌ * مُطَوَّقَةٌ نَاحَتْ فَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَهْلا
لَعَمْرُكَ لَوْ كَانَتْ كَمِثْلِي حَزِينَةً * لَمَا لَبِسَتْ طَوْقًا وَلَا خَضَبَتْ رِجْلًا
وَفَارَقَنِي اِلْفِي فَلَاقَيْتُ بَعْدَهُ * دَوَاعِيَ هَمِّ لَا تُفَارِقُنِي اَصْلًا
sentences.tr:
ʿalimnā bi-annā baʿda ghaybatikum nublā * wa-maddat qusiyyun li-al-firāqi lanā nablā
wa-qad khallafūnī baʿda shaddi riḥālihim * uʿāliju kurba al-mawti idh qaṭaʿū al-ramlā
laqad hatafat bī junḥa laylin ḥamāmatun * muṭawwaqatun nāḥat fa-qultu lahā mahlā
laʿamruka law kānat ka-mithlī ḥazīnatan * la-mā labisat ṭawqan wa-lā khaḍabat rijlā
wa-fāraqanī ilfī fa-lāqaytu baʿdahu * dawāʿiya hammi lā tufāriqunī aṣlā
sentences.l:
We knew that after your absence we would be worn-away, * and bows stretched for us, for the parting, arrows;
and they left-me-behind after the binding of their saddles, * struggling with the anguish of death when they crossed the sand.
A dove called to me in the wing of a night, * a ringed-one; she lamented, and I said to her: Gently!
By your life, if she were like-as-me grieving, * she would not wear a collar nor dye a foot.
And my intimate parted from me, and I met after him * causes of care that do not part from me at all.
sentences.i:
We knew that once you were gone we would waste away, * that the bows of parting had drawn their arrows on us;
they left me behind when their saddles were bound, * wrestling with the throes of death as they crossed the sands.
In the dark of night a ring-necked dove * called out to me, lamenting; I said to her, “Softly!
By your life, if she grieved as I grieve, * she would wear no collar, and dye no foot.”
My companion has left me, and after him I have met * with causes of grief that will never leave me.
sentences.n: Five lines in the metre ṭawīl, rhyming in -lā, copied as the print points them. The first line plays on nublā, “we are worn away”, and nabl, “arrows”. qusiyy, plural of qaws, “bow”. The poem moves between “you” (ghaybatikum) and “they” (khallafūnī, riḥālihim), as such borrowed laments often do. The print points kurb, “anguish”, where the usual form is karb. The dove's dark neck-ring and red feet are read as finery a true mourner would not wear: ṭawq, “collar”; khaḍaba, “to dye with henna”. ilf, “intimate companion”. The print gives hammi without tanwīn; the sense is dawāʿiya hammin, “causes of care”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا امْتَنَعَتْ مِنَ الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ وَزَادَتْ فِى الْبُكَاءِ وَالِانْتِحَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā imtanaʿat mina al-ṭaʿāmi wa-al-sharābi wa-zādat fī al-bukāʾi wa-al-intiḥābi
sentences.l: Then she refrained from the food and the drink, and increased in the weeping and the sobbing.
sentences.i: After that she refused all food and drink, and wept and sobbed the more.
sentences.n: Rhyme: sharāb, intiḥāb. intiḥāb, “loud weeping, sobbing”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ بُكَاؤُهَا عَلَى رُؤُسِ الْأَشْهَادِ فَأَبْكَتِ الْعِبَادَ وَالْبِلَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra bukāʾuhā ʿalā ruʾūsi al-ashhādi fa-abkati al-ʿibāda wa-al-bilāda
sentences.l: And her weeping became upon the heads of the witnesses, so she made-weep the servants and the lands.
sentences.i: She wept openly before all the world, until she set people and places alike weeping.
sentences.n: Rhyme: ashhād, ʿibād, bilād. ʿalā ruʾūsi al-ashhādi, “over the heads of the witnesses”, means “in public, before everyone”, a common idiom. The print spells ruʾūs with one wāw (رؤس). al-ʿibād, “the servants (of God)”, is “mankind”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ النَّاسُ يَقُولُونَ أَيْنَ عَيْنُكَ يَا ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَشَكَوْا تَحَامُلَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra al-nāsu yaqūlūna ayna ʿaynuka yā ḍawʾa al-makāni wa-shakaw taḥāmula al-zamāni
sentences.l: And the people began saying: Where is your eye, O Ḍawʾ al-Makān? And they complained of the oppression of the time.
sentences.i: And people began to say, “Ḍawʾ al-Makān, if only you could see!” and they complained of the cruelty of fortune.
sentences.n: ayna ʿaynuka, “where is your eye?”: if only you were here to see it. They address the dead father. Rhyme: makān, zamān. taḥāmul ʿalā, “to bear down unjustly on”: the time's oppression.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا يَا هَلْ تَرَى مَا جَرَى عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ حَتَّى بَعُدَ عَنْ وَطَنِهِ وَطُرِدَ مِنَ الْمَكَانِ وَكَانَ أَبُوهُ يُشْبِعُ الْجِيعَانَ وَيَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَالْأَمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū yā hal tarā mā jarā ʿalā kāna mā kāna ḥattā baʿuda ʿan waṭanihi wa-ṭurida mina al-makāni wa-kāna abūhu yushbiʿu al-jīʿāna wa-yaʾmuru bi-al-ʿadli wa-al-amāni
sentences.l: And they said: O, do you see what befell Kān Mā Kān, so that he went-far from his homeland and was driven from the place? And his father used to fill the hungry and command justice and safety.
sentences.i: And they said, “What, we wonder, has befallen Kān Mā Kān, that he should go so far from home, driven out of his own place, when his father fed the hungry and ordained justice and security?”
sentences.n: yā hal tarā, “O, do you see?”, a colloquial “I wonder”. jarā ʿalā, “to befall”. jīʿān, “hungry”, is a colloquial form (Classical jāʾiʿ or jawʿān). amara bi-, “to command”: bi- marks what is ordered. Rhyme: makān, jīʿān, amān.

sentences.t: وَزَادَتْ أُمُّهُ فِى الْبُكَاءِ وَالْآنَانِ فَوَصَلَ الْخَبَرُ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-zādat ummuhu fī al-bukāʾi wa-al-ānāni fa-waṣala al-khabaru ilā al-maliki sāsāna
sentences.l: And his mother increased in the weeping and the moaning, and the news reached al-Malik Sāsān.
sentences.i: His mother wept and moaned the more, and the news reached al-Malik Sāsān.
sentences.n: The word printed الآنان is doubtful. It is kept as printed and read as a word for moaning, rhyming with Sāsān: most likely the verbal noun unān (from anna, yaʾinnu, “to moan”), with the madda set by the print, or a slip for anīn, “moaning”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
